eras.note: ERCOT nodal market go-live. HCAP was $2,250/MWh (not $3,000) and no ORDC existed yet; the archive never exceeds $2,429 in this window.
HCAP stepped to $3,000 two months after nodal opening per 16 TAC 25.505(g)(6)(D); the Feb 2 2011 rolling outages and the Aug 2011 heat both price to this cap.
Interim HCAP set by the standalone rule 16 TAC 25.508 (PUCT Project 37897), adopted after the June 25 2012 open meeting.
NPRR385 added the administrative Settlement Point Price floor of -$251/MWh in RTM and DAM; the -$250 Energy Offer Curve floor was unchanged. No panel interval is below -$251 from this date on.
First step of the PUCT Project 40268 schedule; the same order set the LCAP and a $300k/MW-yr peaker-net-margin threshold.

eras.ordc_change: ORDC introduced (RTORPA / RTOFFPA real-time price adders)
eras.note: ORDC went live under NPRR568 with VOLL equal to the SWCAP and a 2,000 MW minimum contingency level. ERCOT's reports say only 'June 2014'; 2014-06-01 is high-confidence, not literal-quote-confirmed.
Final step of the Project 40268 schedule; PNM threshold moved to $315k/MW-yr (3x CONE).

eras.ordc_change: ORDC Mu shifted up by 0.25 sigma
eras.note: First of two PUCT-directed rightward shifts of the LOLP distribution mean (the mean moves, not sigma). PUCT directed it 2019-01-17; the ERCOT Board approved 2019-02-12. Aug 13 and Aug 15 2019 both price to the $9,000 cap.

eras.ordc_change: ORDC Mu shifted up a further 0.25 sigma (0.50 sigma cumulative)
eras.note: Second shift, implemented via OBDRR011. This is the ORDC configuration in force during Winter Storm Uri (Feb 2021).

eras.ordc_change: VOLL dropped to $2,000 with the offer cap
eras.note: The only time the LCAP has ever bound. Peaker net margin crossed the threshold on Operating Day 2021-02-16 but PUCT emergency orders suspended the switch until Operating Day 2021-03-04 (DAM from 03-05). The archive agrees: max $3,306 after 2021-03-04 versus $10,530 during Uri.

eras.ordc_change: Minimum contingency level raised 2,000 MW -> 3,000 MW; VOLL reset to $5,000
eras.note: HCAP cut from $9,000 to $5,000 by PUCT Project 52631 (Dec 2 2021 open meeting). VOLL follows automatically because 25.505(g)(6)(E) ties VOLL to the offer cap in effect, so the MCL increase was adopted as an offset.

eras.ordc_change: Multi-step RTORPA price-adder floors added ($20/MWh at RTOLCAP <= 6,500 MW; $10/MWh at <= 7,000 MW)
eras.note: ECRS also launched 2023-06-10 as a new ancillary service, materially changing observed scarcity pricing inside this era.

Emergency Pricing Program live: if the system-wide price sits at or above HCAP for 12 hours in a rolling 24, an emergency cap of $2,000/MWh replaces both the cap and VOLL. 16 TAC 25.509 (PUCT Project 54585), from SB 3 section 18.

eras.ordc_change: ORDC price adders retired, replaced by co-optimized Ancillary Service Demand Curves
eras.note: RTC+B go-live split the cap: DASWCAP $5,000/MWh and RTSWCAP $2,000/MWh. hcap here is the real-time cap, which is what the RTM panel is bounded by. VOLL for the ASDCs stays at the DAM cap of $5,000.

meta.price: mean of HB_HOUSTON, HB_NORTH, HB_SOUTH, HB_WEST (HB_HUBAVG-equivalent, HB_PAN excluded)

finding: SUPPRESSION, not scarcity reduction. The grid is physically tighter than it has ever been: peak net load rose from 66.5 GW (2011) to 75.6 GW (2026), and net load above 70 GW -- which never once happened in 2011-2022 (0.0 h) -- has now occurred in every year since 2023 (9.5 h total).

What collapsed is the conversion of tightness into price. Comparing only physically comparable years (>= 25 h above 65 GW), P(RT >= $500 | net load in the year's top 0.5%) averaged 0.41 in 2011-2023 and 0.09 in 2024-2026; conditioned on the absolute >= 65 GW cut it fell from 0.41 to 0.10. 2025 is the extreme case: 25.2 h above 65 GW and a 71.0 GW peak, and not one of those intervals priced at $500.

The cleanest single comparison is the 70 GW cut, the only level on which 2023 and 2026 are the same physical event: 2023 had 2.5 h above 70 GW (n=10 intervals) and priced 1.00 of them at >= $500; 2026 has 4.8 h (n=19) -- nearly twice as many -- and priced 0.00. 2025 priced its 3 such intervals at zero. Small n (10/6/3/19 intervals across 2023-2026), so this is the corroborating comparison, not the load-bearing one.

Be precise about what this is NOT: the conditional has no monotone trend over the panel (Mann-Kendall tau=+0.17, p=0.39); it was already near zero in 2014, 2016 and 2017, which were loose years. This is a LEVEL SHIFT conditional on tightness, not a drift. Hours above 65 GW did fall from the 2023 record (72.2 h) to 28.8/25.2/25.0 h, so some genuine loosening is real -- but 2024-2026 still runs above the 2011-2022 average (13.4 h). Suppression (ECRS 2023-06, RTORPA floors 2023-11, the Emergency Pricing Program 2023-12, RTC+B and a $2,000 RT cap 2025-12) explains the residual.

Events moved, decisively and in the direction solar predicts. Mean $500 event start hour went from 13.1 h (2011-2015, n=156) to 15.9 h (2022-2026, n=149); two-sample KS D=0.278, p=1.0e-05. The share of >= $500 intervals in the 18-21 h net-peak ramp went from 0.07 (2011) to 0.74 (2026), while the 13-17 h afternoon share went from 0.72 to 0.00. Scarcity is now an evening-ramp phenomenon, not an afternoon one.

The storage fingerprint is ABSENT, and its absence is the interesting part. Batteries clip the tail of an event, so 17 GW of mostly 1-4 h storage should show duration falling with event count flat. Observed is the opposite: median duration rises (Mann-Kendall tau=+0.62, p=0.001) from 0.50 h to 2.25 h, p90 duration rises (tau=+0.44, p=0.019), and events per 8,760 h show no trend (tau=-0.06, p=0.79).

Read that as a threshold effect, not as storage failing: the brief single-interval ORDC-adder spikes that made up most of the old count are gone, and what survives the new pricing apparatus is the small number of genuinely long, deep events -- median duration is now 2.25 h on 5 events, against 0.25 h on 30 in 2013. Depth above $500 does NOT trend (tau=+0.27, p=0.16) and 2026's $500/MWh is the lowest since 2016, so read this as fewer and longer, not deeper.

For the product: pooled over the whole panel, only 0.23 of >= $500 intervals sat in their year's top 0.5% of net load, so price-triggered curtailment was never a clean proxy for physical scarcity even before 2024. Underwriting on $/MWh arbitrage means underwriting a pricing apparatus that the PUCT has now demonstrated it will change -- three times in thirty months. Underwriting on physical tightness (net-load rank, 4CP, interconnection access) is underwriting a trend that is still going the right way.

Caveat on the reserve proxy: dispatchable nameplate never comes within 10.5 GW of net load on this basis, so the 5/3/2 GW reserve-proxy columns are all zero. That is a limitation of nameplate capacity as a stand-in for ERCOT's PRC (it ignores outages, derates and AS commitments), not evidence of a comfortable grid -- use the net-load series, not this column.
